title: POC scoping: benchmark harness integration and load testing
summary: Redwood AE+SE and Acme Health Labs scoped a PoC focused on integrating Acme's benchmark harness with Redwood's hosted/dedicated endpoints. Primary goals: define success criteria (latency and cost targets), agree workload sizing and test scripts, decide streaming vs non-streaming behaviour, and align on timelines for run and analysis.
action_items: Priya: share canonical inference scripts + sample payloads by 2026-06-15
Maya: provide Redwood benchmark harness adapter and README by 2026-06-18
Jordan: send proposed timeline and pricing tiers by 2026-06-14
Liam: confirm network egress rules and VPC peering requirements by 2026-06-16
next_steps: Acme to drop scripts and dataset samples into shared S3 link
Redwood to fork Acme harness and submit PR with adapter and example configs
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-06-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Carlos Rivera (Acme CTO), Priya Singh (Acme ML Engineer), Liam O'Connor (Acme Infra)
---
[15:01] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Today we're focused on the PoC scope for the benchmark harness integration, load profiles, and what success looks like. Can we do quick intros?
[15:02] Carlos: Carlos here, I'm the CTO, overseeing infra and timeline. We're hoping to validate inference economics for our clinical summarization feature—latency under 350 ms p95 and cost tolerable against GPU-on-demand.
[15:03] Priya: Priya, ML Eng. I'll own the scripts and dataset for the benchmarks, plus metrics. We'll be using about 1.2k average tokens per request for the longer summaries and a tail of 4k tokens for some transcripts.
[15:04] Liam: Liam on infra, I'll handle network access and any VPC peering. We're sensitive about PHI and need encryption + audit logs.
[15:04] Jordan: Great, Maya and I will run the integration. Maya, do you want to frame what the Redwood harness adapters look like?
[15:05] Maya: Yeah. We typically provide a small adapter that plugs into customer load tools or your Python harness. For folks using locust/jmeter or a custom python runner we'll supply an example that: 1) wraps our REST streaming and non-streaming endpoints, 2) does token accounting, 3) records latency histograms and token cost per request. We can also run the harness from our side to reproduce results.
[15:06] Priya: Question: do you support SSE streaming and chunked responses in the harness? Our client-side UI streams as tokens arrive, so streaming behaviour affects perceived latency and concurrency math.
[15:07] Maya: Yes, we test both. There are two modes we want to capture: streaming (SSE or chunked HTTP) and non-streaming (complete response). Streaming impacts load testing because you hold a connection open longer at lower immediate throughput. For concurrency you need to simulate sustained connections rather than short bursts.
[15:08] Carlos: So for our goal of p95 < 350 ms, is that measured for first token or end-to-end? In our case, UX wants first-token under 200 ms for short prompts, but full completion for long transcripts isn't realistic.
[15:09] Jordan: Good callout. We'll define success criteria as: first-token p95 < 250 ms for short prompts (<=512 tokens), end-to-end p95 < 1.5s for average 1.2k token jobs, and cost-per-1k-tokens under $X (TBD as part of pricing). We'll make those explicit in the PoC doc.
[15:10] Priya: For workload sizing, we anticipate 250 RPS peak across our service, with a median concurrency of ~40 active requests. The load pattern is bursty—morning batch and then patient-initiated requests. We'll provide real traffic traces.
[15:11] Maya: For the harness we'll need: sample payloads, tokenization behaviour (are you using gpt-tokenizer or custom), and a traffic trace for arrival patterns. We'll parameterize the harness to replay arrival times and to simulate streaming vs non-streaming client behavior.
[15:12] Liam: Network constraints: our infra sits in us-east-1 and we plan to peer to Redwood private endpoints for the dedicated PoC. Would you be able to run the hosted first and then switch to dedicated if we like numbers?
[15:13] Jordan: Absolutely. Typical flow: run hosted quick runs to validate correctness and baseline, then do dedicated runs for steady-state throughput and final cost numbers. We can also show fallback behaviour.
[15:14] Carlos: Security: SOC 2 and SSO/SAML integration questions. We'll need to see audit logs and KMS integration for the dedicated environment.
[15:15] Maya: We support SAML SSO and KMS/HSM for key management on private deployments. For hosted PoC we can demonstrate restricted retention and audit logs and supply our security pack. We'll attach the docs after the call.
[15:17] Priya: About the harness: our current micro-bench uses a small Python runner that calls your API and records latency. It's not set up for high concurrency or streaming. We'd prefer Redwood to adapt our existing runner rather than rewrite tests.
[15:18] Maya: That's fine. The adapter approach: you give us your runner and we'll add a thin module (about ~100 lines) that swaps endpoints and does token accounting. We also include a CI-friendly example that pushes results to a CSV and a histogram.json.
[15:20] Jordan: Timeline proposals—what timeline are you targeting for PoC scope and run?
[15:20] Carlos: We want results in about three weeks; internal sign-off takes another week, so total ~4 weeks if things look good.
[15:21] Maya: Proposed schedule: 6/15 Redwood receives scripts and sample data; 6/18 Redwood delivers adapter + README; 6/22 kickoff engineer-to-engineer to run the harness; 6/23-6/26 run broad benchmarks (hosted), 6/29 run dedicated tests and regression; 7/1 deliver final report. Does that align?
[15:22] Priya: That seems reasonable. We might need an extra day for the big transcript samples.
[15:24] Liam: Questions about load testing specifics: How do you account for KV cache and prefix caching in your costs? Our workload has high token overlap.
[15:25] Maya: We record cache hit rates and can run two profiles: cold-cache and warm-cache. The harness can pre-warm by replaying prefixes to populate KV cache before the measured run. That will show the delta in tokens served and effective cost-per-call. We'll mark runs as cold/warm in the results.
[15:27] Priya: Another concern: quantization/profile variants. We'll test a few model variants: redwood-v2-7b-quant, redwood-v2-13b-fp16 (approx names), and a smaller 3B fallback. We want latency and cost tradeoffs captured.
[15:28] Maya: We can run those. Note: kernel selection and sequence length can change throughput. We'll capture per-model p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec. Also include errors and truncations.
[15:30] Jordan: On the client-side streaming tests, to emulate your UI we need two modes: 1) first-token latency (measure time-to-first-byte) and 2) streaming throughput (tokens/sec delivered). For load tests we should script simulated open connections for streaming to reflect sustained concurrency.
[15:32] Carlos: Do you throttle or limit connections differently for streaming endpoints? We worry about connection storms from mobile clients.
[15:33] Maya: Streaming endpoints are connection-based; rate limiting counts active connections and tokens. We'll share recommended throttling policies. We can param the harness to simulate backoffs and retries to mimic mobile behaviour.
[15:35] Priya: For the harness output format, can you produce CSV plus JSON with histograms and a short summary so our analytics team can ingest it?
[15:36] Maya: Yes CSV for raw events and JSON for aggregated histograms. We'll include a summary with cost-per-1k-tokens estimate using your token mix.
[15:38] Jordan: Pricing note—I'll send a tiered proposal for hosted and dedicated PoC pricing. For dedicated we offered reserved pool pricing during our last conversation which will be in the email.
[15:39] Carlos: We might also need legal one-pager for data processing addendum.
[15:40] Jordan: We'll attach DPA and SOC 2 summary.
[15:41] Priya: One more technical: how do you handle streaming vs non-streaming for token accounting? If a stream produces tokens incrementally, do you charge as produced tokens or as response tokens?
[15:42] Maya: We charge for tokens produced, so streaming doesn't change token billing—just the timing. For benchmarking, we'll report both billable tokens and observed latency.
[15:44] Liam: For the dedicated run with VPC peering, will Redwood provide endpoint IPs or DNS entries? We'll need to allow traffic through our firewall.
[15:45] Maya: We'll provide a short list of egress IPs and TLS certificates for the private endpoint and a runbook for peering.
[15:47] Priya: On data masking—some of our transcripts contain PHI. During tests, we will mask names and identifiers; still need assurance logs don't retain sensitive text.
[15:48] Jordan: We'll ensure retention controls for the PoC and annotate the PoC agreement with no persistent retention beyond the test window.
[15:50] Maya: A technical gotcha: if you run long streaming sessions, some load tools interpret the connection as idle; we recommend using tools that support streaming (e.g., our harness, a patched locust, or a python async runner). We'll provide examples.
[15:52] Carlos: OK, let's summarize the concrete deliverables and owners.
[15:53] Jordan: Recap: 1) Priya: upload scripts + sample payloads by 6/15. 2) Maya: deliver adapter + README by 6/18. 3) Jordan: pricing and PoC doc by 6/14. 4) Liam: confirm VPC/firewall details by 6/16. 5) Schedule kickoff for week of 6/22.
[15:55] Priya: Sounds good. Also, will Redwood run an initial short sanity-run so we confirm configuration?
[15:56] Maya: Yes, small sanity-run once adapter is wired, then full runs. We'll also run cold-then-warm cache runs.
[15:57] Carlos: Any blockers on Redwood's side?
[15:58] Maya: None beyond receiving your scripts and access. For dedicated we'll need a contact for peering.
[15:59] Jordan: I'll follow up with a combined email with timeline, attachments (security docs), and a shared S3 link for the sample data.
[16:00] Carlos: Thanks all, looking forward.
---
Notes: occasional transcription artifacts present (e.g., KV cache may be transcribed "K V cache", product names approximated). Attachments to be sent: security pack, DPA, adapter README, pricing proposal.
